title: גַּאֲוָה וַעֲנָוָה – גְּנוּת הַגַּאֲוָה וּמַעֲלַת הָעֲנָוָה
hebrewTitle: גַּאֲוָה וַעֲנָוָה – גְּנוּת הַגַּאֲוָה וּמַעֲלַת הָעֲנָוָה

segments.he: א. לִפְעָמִים הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע רוֹצֶה לְהַכְנִיס גַּאֲוָה, חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, בְּלֵב הַצַּדִּיק, בַּאֲשֶׁר הוּא צַדִּיק מוֹשֵׁל בְּיִרְאַתשׂאֱלֹקִים, וְכִבְיָכוֹל רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּיָדוֹ, כִּי מִי מוֹשֵׁל בִּי? - צַדִּיק; אֲזַי צָרִיךְ לְהָשִׁיב אֶל לִבּוֹ דָּבָר זֶה בְּעַצְמוֹ וְלוֹמַר: אֵיךְ אֲנִי מוֹשֵׁל כְּשֶׁיֶּשׁ לִי גַּאֲוָה וְאֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שׁוֹרֶה עִמִּי, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַזַ"ל (ליקו"מ קז).

ב. אֵין זֶה מִמִּדַּת עֲנָוָה לִהְיוֹת שָׁפָל וְנִבְזֶה וְלֹא יִהְיֶה בּוֹ שׁוּם עַזּוּת דִּקְדֻשָּׁה, כִּי אֵין לָאָדָם חֵלֶק בַּתּוֹרָה כְּשֶׁאֵין בּוֹ עַזּוּת דִּקְדֻשָּׁה לַעֲמֹד נֶגֶד כָּל הַקָּמִים עָלָיו לִמְנֹעַ אוֹתוֹ מֵעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, חַס וְשָׁלוֹם. וְעִקַּר מִדַּת הָעֲנָוָה בִּשְׁלֵמוּת הוּא, כְּשֶׁהוּא בְּמַדְרֵגָה שֶׁיּוּכַל לִכְתֹּב עַל עַצְמוֹ כְּמוֹ משֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ, עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: "וְהָאִישׁ משֶׁה עָנָו מְאֹד" - זֶהוּ מַדְרֵגַת הָעֲנָוָה בְּתַכְלִית, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁמָּצִינוּ בָּאָמוֹרָאִים, שֶׁאָמַר רַב יוֹסֵף: לָא תִתְּנֵי עֲנָוָה, דְּאִיכָּא אֲנָא (שם קמז).

ג. עֲנָוָה בְּלֹא חָכְמָה אֵינָהּ כְּלוּם. כִּי בְּוַדַּאי אֵין זֶה מַעֲלַת הָעֲנָוָה לְהַרְאוֹת עַצְמוֹ בִּכְפִיפַת רֹאשׁ בְּדֶרֶךְ שְׁטוּת כְּאִלּוּ הוּא עָנָו, כִּי זֶהוּ עֲנָוָה פְּסוּלָה. וְעִקַּר שְׁלֵמוּת הָעֲנָוָה - כְּשֶׁהוּא בְּחָכְמָה. וְעַל יְדֵי פְּגַם לָשׁוֹן הָרָע שֶׁל הָעוֹלָם נַעֲשֶֹׁה פֵּרוּד בֵּין עֲנָוָה לְחָכְמָה, וְאָז אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת עָנָו בִּשְׁלֵמוּת, אִם לֹא מִי שֶׁהוּא בְּמַעֲלָה גְדוֹלָה מְאֹד בְּמִדַּת הָעֲנָוָה, עַד שֶׁגַּם פְּגַם לָשׁוֹן הָרָע שֶׁל הָעוֹלָם אֵינוֹ מַזִּיק לוֹ לַעֲנָוָה שֶׁלּוֹ (שם קצז).

ד. כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם מַעְלִים וּמַסְתִּיר וּמַקְטִין אֶת עַצְמוֹ בַּעֲנָוָה וְשִׁפְלוּת, אֲזַי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כִּבְיָכוֹל גַּם כֵּן מַרְאֶה עַצְמוֹ אֵלָיו בִּבְחִינַת עֲנָוָה וְשִׁפְלוּת, וּמְצַמְצֵם אֶת גַּאֲוָתוֹ וּגְאוֹנוֹ וּמַקְטִין אֶת עַצְמוֹ כִּבְיָכוֹל וְשׁוֹכֵן עִמּוֹ בִּבְחִינַת 'אֶשְׁכֹּן אֶת דַּכָּא'. אֲבָל כְּשֶׁהָאָדָם מִתְגָּאֶה וּמִתְגַּדֵּל, חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, אֲזַי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ גַּם כֵּן מַרְאֶה גַּאֲוָתוֹ וְגָדְלוֹ, אֲשֶׁר מִי יוּכַל לִסְבֹּל וּלְקַבֵּל כְּבוֹדוֹ וְגַאֲוָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּי הִנֵּה הַשָּׁמַיִם וּשְׁמֵי הַשָּׁמַיִם לֹא יְכַלְכְּלוּךָ וְכוּ'. וּמִזֶּה בָּא חֻרְבַּן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, בַּעֲוֹנוֹתֵינוּ הָרַבִּים (שם ריט).

ה. יֵשׁ אֶחָד שֶׁהוּא עָנָו, וְאֵין הָעֲנָוָה בַּלֵּב אוֹ בְּאֵיזֶה אֵיבָר מִשְּׁאָר הָאֵיבָרִים. וְעִקַּר שְׁלֵמוּת הָעֲנָוָה הוּא, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה עָנָו בְּתַכְלִית בְּכָל הָאֵיבָרִים, שֶׁלִּבּוֹ וְכָל אֵיבָרָיו יִהְיוּ בִּבְחִינַת עֲנָוָה בְּתַכְלִית הַבִּטּוּל.
ו. עַל יְדֵי שִׁפְלוּת זוֹכִין לֶאֱמוּנָה (ספר המדות).

ז. דֶּרֶךְ הֶעָנָו, שֶׁבְּכָל מַה שֶּׁמְּשַׁבְּחִין וּמְגַדְּלִין אוֹתוֹ יוֹתֵר, הוּא בָּא בַּעֲנִיווּת וּבְקַטְנוּת יוֹתֵר, בִּבְחִינַת "בִּמְקוֹם גְּדֻלָּתוֹ שָׁם אַתָּה מוֹצֵא עַנְוְתָנוּתוֹ" (סיפומע"ש).
segments.en:
And when G-d seems to be pushing one away — feel shame for doubting His mercy, and begin again.

Strengthen your fellow (§ 7): The person who cannot strengthen himself can still strengthen his fellow — and paradoxically, this itself becomes the path back to his own service of G-d.

Even temporary closeness counts (§ 8): A flash of genuine drawing-close, even followed by a fall, is precious in G-d's eyes. Nothing is wasted.

Two teachings on the infinite regress of Divine unknowability. §1 presents a paradox that deepens with each reading: the highest spiritual attainment — "the ultimate of knowledge is that we do not know" — is itself only a relative ultimate, valid only for one's current level. Above it lies another level, with its own unknowable ultimate, and so on without end. True knowledge begins precisely where the certainty of knowing ends. §2 maps this onto the intellectual landscape: philosophy reaches the celestial spheres and stops, imagining there is only raw Divine essence above. Kabbalah begins exactly there. And even Kabbalah has no ceiling — *His greatness is unfathomable*.

Six teachings on the spiritual danger of secular philosophical inquiry — and the infinite superiority of Torah. The chapter's central argument is structural: philosophy's ceiling is Kabbalah's floor (§1, cf. Ch. 14 §2). The investigative books do not create righteous people — they give ammunition to the inborn inclination toward wickedness (§2). Every human innovation, however, originates in a flash from above: Torah scholars receive their illumination through holiness; philosophers through the Sitra Achra (§2). New philosophy produces new diseases (§3). And the decree to teach children external wisdoms is singled out as the most dangerous of all decrees — more threatening than physical persecution — because it uproots faith from within (§6).

Two teachings on the hidden spiritual logic of travel and displacement. §1 reveals that the mysterious, seemingly irrational urge to travel is often the soul's self-preservation instinct — the mazal perceiving a decree that the conscious mind cannot see, and moving the body to safety. The practical lesson: when this urge arises, do not publicize it. §2 opens toward the extraordinary: every journey is a Divine appointment. A simple Jew — not a scholar, not a mystic — rectifies the world wherever he sets foot, simply by performing any holy act in that place. The journey he resists taking may be the very repair his soul came into the world to make.

The largest chapter in the Mahadura Basra — 41 teachings — is fittingly the one on awe and service of G-d. It spans the full arc of spiritual life, from the first moment of entering the straight path to the deepest levels of ratzo v'shov [advance and return]. Several threads stand out:

The intellect in all things (§§ 1–6): The opening series presents a complete Kabbalistic theory of spiritual perception: every created thing contains a holy intellect — a spark of wisdom — and the Jewish person's task is to perceive it and use it as a ladder toward G-d. This is precisely how Yosef withstood his trial. The gateway to this perception is accepting the Kingship of Heaven with complete self-nullification.

Two yetzers / one fire (§ 19): One of the most liberating teachings: serving G-d without a yetzer hara would be incomplete. The task is to take the very fire of the yetzer hara and redirect it entirely into holy service.

The shadow (§§ 16, 30): Deficiencies in children, livelihood, and health are not G-d withholding light — the light flows always. The person's own physicality and deeds create a shadow blocking it. Rectification of deeds removes the shadow.

The Ba'al Tefillah (§§ 39–40): Two teachings summarize the epic twelfth story of the Sipuray Ma'asios — the longest in the book. The world's confusion about the ultimate purpose, the murderer-holiness parable, and the return through prayer are all drawn to their essential conclusion: prayer, humility, and simplicity are the true ultimate purpose. And the Ba'al Tefillah — the master of prayer — is the true king.

Alacrity and patience (§ 41): The final teaching holds both poles simultaneously: act immediately, without delay — and yet sometimes, wait. Both are equally essential. This is the paradox of balanced holy service.

Twenty-two teachings on money — the most multidimensional treatment in any Breslov work. Key threads:

The idolatry of money (§§ 2, 11, 20): The lust for money is literally idolatry — and the most dangerous of all lusts, harder to escape than any other (§20). The very wealthy are generally literally mad (§11). Those sunken in it are immune to rebuke — they treat money as their faith and ultimate purpose.

True wealth from truth (§§ 2–4): The only path to genuine livelihood is emes — the breaking of the lust for money. Faithfulness in business fulfills the root of all mitzvos and elevates the mind to mochin d'gadlus.

The royalty of sustenance (§ 8): Livelihood does not come immediately because it must pass through the King — undergoing clarifications until beautiful utterances [imrei shafer] are formed and crown the King. The circuits and delays of sustenance are not obstacles but the royal process itself.

Contentment (§ 17): One of the most practical teachings: do not force the hour. Wait in trust. Better to be a debtor to oneself than a debtor to others.

The future redemption of money (§ 21): The wondrous foods that will cause all humanity to suddenly see the stench of money — and cast it away — point toward a messianic future in which the distortion of money-worship is entirely reversed.

Seventeen teachings reveal machlokes [dispute/controversy] as one of the most paradoxically productive forces in the spiritual world — not despite being destructive but because of it:

Dispute as Divine protection (§ 2): When a Tzaddik becomes too famous, G-d places it in another tzaddik's heart to oppose him — to shield his light from prosecution. Controversy can be the very mechanism through which shefa reaches the world.

Dispute as building material (§ 13): The scattered stones of dispute become the building blocks of the Tzaddik's worlds — all 310 of them. The more opposition, the more construction material.

The true Tzaddik's response (§§ 6, 12, 15): Judge with the scale of merit. Accept suffering with love. Understand that those who oppose do not even know who they are opposing — they oppose a fiction, not the real Tzaddik.

Dispute and growth (§ 17): The earth must split for the tree to grow. Dispute is the splitting.

Forty-eight teachings across all the sacred times of the Jewish year. Several master themes emerge:

Shabbos as cosmic purpose (§§ 1, 8, 10, 11): Shabbos is not merely a day of rest — it is the ultimate telos of all creation. Israel was created for Shabbos. The additional soul that comes on Shabbos is itself formed through holy yearning. Eating Shabbos food must be for Shabbos holiness alone — not from yesterday's hunger or tomorrow's.

Speech and Shabbos (§ 3): When the generation does not guard their speech, they cannot receive the illumination of Shabbos — even if the Tzaddik transmits it. This connection between guarding speech and receiving Shabbos is one of the deepest in Breslov.

Pesach = Peh Sach (§§ 9, 10): The Exodus is the liberation of speech from exile. Pesach is literally "a mouth that speaks." Livelihood itself flows from this liberated speech. Matzah = strife for Heaven's sake = the highest da'as = peace.

The shofar (§§ 1–5 of Tishrei): The shofar blasts break the boldness of the Sitra Achra, enable the soul to communicate with the body, spread prophecy, and restore lost things — all simultaneously. The three sounds correspond to the three dimensions of heavenly rectification.

Amalek and prayer (Purim §4): Prayer — which transcends nature — is the only weapon that truly subdues Amalek's philosophical heresy. For philosophy operates within the laws of nature; prayer overturns them entirely.

At 121 teachings, this is the longest chapter in all of Likutay Aitzos. It ranges from the most abstract Kabbalistic dimensions of the Tzaddik's role in creation to the most practical guidance on how to draw close to him during and after life. Several overarching themes:

The Tzaddik as cosmic axis (§§ 21, 62, 94): There is one Tzaddik Yesod Olam [Righteous Foundation of the World] in every generation — from whom all four elements, all honor, all sustenance, and all time itself flow. The formation of time itself depends on him gathering true acts of loving-kindness. Every Tzaddik of the generation is a dimension of Moshe-Mashiach.

Concealment and paradox (§§ 44, 65, 91–99): The greatest tzaddikim are the most hidden. They may appear blind, deaf, hunchbacked, or heavy-mouthed — the very names the world gives them [bettlirs, beggars] are their concealment. This extended series based on Story 13 of the Sipuray Ma'asios is one of the most extraordinary passages in all Breslov literature.

Drawing close (§§ 87, 101, 108): The teaching that after the true Tzaddik is present in the world, one cannot draw close to G-d truly except through him (§108) is among the most characteristic Breslov teachings. And the drawing-close continues after death — even in the World to Come, wicked souls who manage to reach the Tzaddik are saved from the sling of the hollow (§101).

The Tzaddik's self-renewal (§ 68): The truly great Tzaddik never rests at one level — each time he attains a new height, he immediately forgets it and begins again as a total beginner. This perpetual beginning is the secret of his perpetual ascent.

Stories as medicine (§ 35): When Torah teachings cannot be received, the Tzaddik must clothe them in external stories. And when even other Torah words fail, the Sipuray Ma'asios — the stories — operate from a dimension that can reach where nothing else can.

This chapter reveals Eretz Yisroel not merely as a geographical location but as the supreme spiritual archetype — the place where hashgachah and emes converge most fully. Several threads run through all eleven teachings:

1. Truth is the root of the Land (§ 1): Eretz Yisroel receives its shefa from emes — the quality of Yaakov-Tiferes. This is why G-d's eyes are "always upon it": falsehood cannot stand before His gaze. Poverty, shame, and social dependency are the symptoms of a damaged connection to this truth-shefa.

2. Providence is its essence (§§ 3–4): What makes the Land holy is not its soil but that Hashem's hashgachah operates there directly, without the veil of nature. The future redemption will extend this condition to the whole world.

3. The path is unearned grace (§ 5): The conquest of the Land cannot be earned — it is matnas chinam, pure gift. Moshe's plea va'eschanan (from the root chinam) models the only correct posture: radical dependence on G-d's generosity.

4. The paradox of ascent (§ 9): The higher the tzaddik's destination, the deeper the humility required to get there. Gadlus d'gadlus demands katnus d'katnus. This is one of the most psychologically profound teachings in all of Breslov.

5. Simple people have an advantage (§ 10): The adversarial force targets greatness. The wholesome and simple are, paradoxically, freer to simply go.

Though brief — four teachings — this chapter delivers a complete spiritual-practical teaching on food. The central insight is that eating is not neutral: it either elevates or degrades the da'as — the innermost faculty of Divine connection. Animal-quality eating severs the link to authentic love and awe of G-d (§ 1). The Tzaddik's eating, by contrast, is an act of soul-polishing that generates emunah (§ 2). The practical corrective is physical: bypassing the pleasure of the palate (§ 3). The warning against raw onions (§ 4) is left opaque here with a cross-reference to the primary text.

The holy sigh is one of the most intimate and accessible spiritual tools in Breslov — it requires no preparation, no knowledge, and no words. These five teachings reveal its multi-layered power:

Healing (§ 1): The sigh heals the life-pulse itself — damaged by the burden of earning a livelihood — and opens a channel to da'as.

Renewal (§ 2): It is a tool of total rebirth — body and soul — not merely comfort.

Ascent (§ 3): Even those already rooted in holiness can use the sigh to climb higher. It is not only a remedy for falling.

Physical reality of spiritual depth (§ 4): The truly authentic sigh is so powerful it physically exhausts the body. The Talmudic tradition is cited: the sigh literally "breaks" a person. And yet — even an ordinary sigh, offered with sincerity, carries great virtue.

Bedtime practice (§ 5): Rebbe Nachman's most practical instruction: if you cannot find words in prayer, sigh. Make it a habit — especially at the vulnerable, intimate moment of lying down to sleep.

Nine teachings on charity. A notable feature of this chapter is that all but §§4 and 8 lack source citations in this edition — suggesting these may be shorter oral traditions preserved without literary attribution.

The key teachings: Tzedakah rectifies the instruments of action (§1) and thereby clears the intellect. It corresponds to the sun (§5) — the weekday sun being the sun of this era, the Shabbos charity corresponding to the great light of the future. The cosmic teaching (§8) — that time itself is formed through true acts of loving-kindness — connects directly to the great story of the spring and the heart in the Sipuray Ma'asios. The copyist's note in §8 is one of the most practically urgent in the entire book.

Five teachings on holy will and longing — brief in number but immense in depth. The chapter draws heavily on the Sipuray Ma'asios, particularly Story 13 (the Seven Beggars) and its extraordinary account of the heart and the spring.

The heart and the spring (§5): The most cosmically urgent teaching in this chapter. The heart of the world cannot reach the spring — but its very yearning and gazing from afar is what keeps it alive; and that vitality sustains all of creation. The lesson: the longing itself, even without fulfillment, is life-giving. This is one of Rebbe Nachman's most original teachings about the spiritual power of unfulfilled holy desire.

The will and the compelled (§2): Even when one is truly unable to perform a mitzvah — the strong will to do it is itself very good, and should not be abandoned by invoking the principle of ones Rachmana patrei [G-d exempts the compelled] as an excuse for spiritual cooling.

Seven teachings on healing (the source skips the number seven in its own numbering, proceeding from §6 to §8). Several are brief aphorisms without source citations.

Illness as dispute (§1): All disease is fundamentally a failure of inner peace — the elements warring within. Healing is peace. This frames the entire chapter: the path to physical healing runs through the same spiritual forces as the path to peace between people and nations.

The soul and medicine (§3): A remarkable teaching: the soul returns to inhabit the body more fully when it sees the person demonstrating the capacity for self-discipline through accepting bitter medicine. The soul reasons: if he can force himself for physical health, he can force himself for spiritual truth.

Shir HaShirim as medicine (§8): All healings are contained in the Song of Songs — reciting it before daybreak when someone is ill. One of the most direct practical prescriptions in the book.

The missing §7: The jump from §6 to §8 appears in the original source itself — this is a scribal or printing anomaly in the Mahadura Basra manuscript, not a gap in this translation.

Eight teachings on joy — only one carries a source citation (§7). The chapter reveals joy as a spiritual technology with precise cosmic effects, not merely a feeling.

Joy and the sparks (§4): Every deficiency a person experiences traces back to the breaking of the vessels — the cosmic disaster of creation. Rejoicing in G-d lifts the fallen sparks and fills the deficiencies. This makes joy not a luxury but a repair operation of the highest order.

The stature of joy (§5): Joy is a complete body — 248 limbs, 365 sinews, one for each mitzvah. Walking through this stature when joyful causes one to stumble precisely at the limb corresponding to a sin one has committed — thereby discovering forgotten sins organically, through joy rather than through suffering.

The paradox of sadness about not being joyful (§6): One of the most psychologically astute teachings in the book. The Rabbis' warnings to be joyful can themselves become a source of sadness. The answer: even the mere will to be joyful is already very good — and can become the seed of actual joy.

Seven teachings on peace. Only §5 carries a source citation; the rest appear to be terse oral traditions.

Love as acoustic phenomenon (§1): A striking opening teaching: the physical propagation of sound through air is the physical analogue of how love propagates Torah. Hatred disrupts the airstreams; love calms them. The Tzaddik's words reach distant lands because the love of his followers smooths the air.

Unity and Divine oneness (§5): The most theologically profound teaching: when many people of differing views unite in love and arrive together at one true holy view — this reveals in the world how all the multiplicity of creation flows from One. This is the deepest reason why unity is precious to G-d.

Shalom bayis (§7): The most practically urgent teaching: the ba'al davar's primary target is the peace of young couples. The two Talmudic citations in this paragraph — "it is sufficient that they raise our children" and "honor your wives" — are preserved and transliterated.

Thirty-four teachings on Torah study — among the richest chapters in the book. Nearly all lack source citations. Several major themes:

The dew of Torah (§10): Torah that does not rise to the Shechinah scatters through the world's atmosphere. Worthy people absorb it as Torah dew — innovations and awakening. Unworthy people absorb the same Torah and it becomes in them the energy of the thirty-nine labors — secular toil. The same spiritual substance produces opposite effects depending on the recipient.

The chambers of Torah (§12): Innovation in Torah is a journey through inner chambers. But the greatest danger is mistaking one's location — believing one has reached the innermost sanctuary when one stands entirely outside. The greatest Tzaddik does not make this mistake: his every attainment seems to him as nothing.

Learning fast vs. learning deep (§27): The Talmudic principle ligmar inish v'hadar lisbar — study first, reflect afterward — enshrines the virtue of broad, rapid study over slow, painstaking analysis. Rebbe Nachman applies it as a general practice for spiritual health.

Kabbalah — a double warning (§34): Two opposite dangers: studying Kabbalah prematurely destroys the heart's feeling in prayer; but for many people it is a great obligation. One must pray to be shown the right path.

The source numbers in §§12 and 20 appear in the original as bare numerals (245 and 353) rather than book-and-chapter references — preserved as such in this translation.

Twenty-eight teachings on prayer — by far the fullest chapter on this topic in the book. The cross-reference numbers תטו [§415] in §10 and תיז [§417] in §21 appear mid-sentence in the source — retained in their correct positions as inline cross-references. The source number רלז [§237] at the end of §28 is a closing citation. The Yiddish term kaave (coffee) in §20 and gizegenen zich (taking leave) in §25 are preserved.

Key teachings: Foreign thoughts during prayer are fallen holy sparks (§6) — and merely wishing to elevate them already breaks the masters of dispute. Prayer's relationship to nature: it overturns it (§10). The sign of holy vs. impure suffering: whether prayer remains possible (§4). And §25 — the cosmic description of Minchah and Ma'ariv as the moment the heart and the spring take leave of each other — one of the most beautiful in the entire book.

Nine teachings on wholeness and simplicity — the final chapter of the Mahadura Basra. Nearly all draw on Story 9 of the Sipuray Ma'asios: the tale of the Chacham v'Tam. The cross-reference numbers and Yiddish-Slavic terms are preserved: prostik (§3), v'chulu instances in §§3, 8 (twice), 9 (twice) — all rendered.

The book ends as it began — with faith. The Wise Man who follows only his own intellect spirals into heresy, loses his father's house (faith), and ends in denial even of the Ba'al Shem Tov. The Simple Man inherits his father's house — holy faith — and from that foundation rises to wisdom greater than the Wise Man's, becomes a righteous judge, a sage in all seven wisdoms, and one who can receive light from every single person, even the most degraded. Temimus is not the absence of wisdom — it is the condition that makes true wisdom possible.

This concludes the translation of the complete Likutay Aitzos Mahadura Basra (ליקוטי עצות מהדורא בתרא) — the Final Edition of the Collection of Advice of Rebbe Nachman of Breslov, of blessed memory.

Forty-six chapters. From Emes v'Emunah — Truth and Faith — to Temimus — Wholeness. Beginning and ending with faith. May this translation bring merit to all who study it, to the soul of the Rebbe, and to the speedy complete redemption.
